name: CHRONIA
blurb: An atlas of the world’s borders from 3400 BC to today. Move through time and watch empires rise and fall. Click any state, people, or settlement on the map for details. Created by weaving public datasets together by our team of historical researchers.
tagline: An atlas of the world’s borders from 3400 BC to today, where you can watch empires rise and fall.

sections.title: Technical details
paragraphs: Before 1886 the borders come from Cliopatria, the Seshat project’s dataset of polities back to 3400 BC, with its gaps filled from dated snapshot maps. From 1886 they come from CShapes 2.0, dated to the day, and the main changes from 1800 to 1885 are dated to the day as well, from the Acts of Union to the fall of Mandalay. Every change made by hand, from Gibraltar’s outline to the occupations of the First World War, is recorded with its sources in a public ledger.

The map is drawn on a canvas in UCHRONIA’s Antique style, with relief, rivers, and about 5,000 cities that appear when they became prominent and take the names of their time. A card for any state, people, or city gives what the maps say about it on that date and a short note from a language model, kept and shared with everyone who opens the same card. The zones of control hatch the ground each side held in 23 wars, and where Mexico’s cartels were present.

sections.title: Inspiration
paragraphs: Historians and geographers have built remarkable datasets of the world’s borders, each covering its own stretch of time or part of the map. I wanted to bring them together into one project, and to build the atlas I had always wanted for myself: one place to watch five thousand years of history move across a map, and to stop on any day and see who held what.

sections.title: Technical details
paragraphs: Footprints, roof heights, and years come from NYC Open Data. Satellite and 3D views come from Google’s Photorealistic 3D Tiles, and archive photos open on Urban Archive.

The record started with researched entries for buildings in every Manhattan neighborhood, drawn from Wikipedia and the city’s building historians. It now covers all five boroughs, and anyone signed in can add to it.

sections.title: Inspiration
paragraphs: Walk past almost any building in New York and there is no way to find out what happened inside it. I wanted a map where every building has a record: what it was, who was there, and what it saw.

sections.title: Technical details
paragraphs: The globe and the flat map are drawn on a canvas from Natural Earth’s states and provinces, with geoBoundaries’ counties and districts for 40 large countries, so a border can follow a county line. Each country’s name is fitted to its shape and, in the Antique style, bent along it; rivers, lakes, 3,000 cities and 40,000 towns are placed so that nothing collides.

The historian is Claude, behind a small server function that holds the key. It reads a plain list of how your map differs from ours, and redraws by sending back edits in a fixed shape, regions changing hands, new countries, subjects, and capitals, which the page applies as one step that a single undo takes back. A shared map travels inside its own link, so nothing is stored on a server.

sections.title: Inspiration
paragraphs: I have been fond of atlases, world history, alternate history, and cartography for as long as I can remember. I built the tool I had always wanted for making my own maps and fictional worlds. I hope UCHRONIA encourages people to learn more about the world, both the real one and the imagined one.

blurb: Preserving the Fuzhounese dialect. The world’s first collaborative Fuzhounese–English dictionary. With 3,790 entries and growing, we are also gathering native-speaker audio to train a language model to ensure the sound of the language never disappears.

sections.title: Technical details
paragraphs: The dictionary has an assistant, powered by Claude, that answers questions based on the content in the dictionary such as: "translate 'have you eaten?' in Fuzhounese", "how many meanings does 'siah' have?", or "explain tone sandhi". Since Fuzhounese varies noticeably from town to town, the dictionary was designed to accommodate variants of words and pronunciations from across the Fuzhounese-speaking world.

sections.title: Inspiration
paragraphs: Fuzhounese is the dialect my family speaks, and there was no English dictionary of it online—or one that emphasized the geographical diversity of the language. I wanted a place to preserve the words and the way variety of ways native speakers voice them. The goal of the project is to serve Fuzhounese speakers, curious language learners, and linguists alike.

sections.title: Technical details
paragraphs: Leggio translates with the latest translation models built into Chrome, so the words you select are translated on your own computer, immediately and for free. You can also plug in your own API key if you'd prefer DeepL or Google Cloud translations.

No data goes to a server, no account required, no analytics tracked, and no ads included. Built-in 'saved words' functionality allows users to build word and phrase lists for better studying and easy export to flash card tools.

sections.title: Inspiration
paragraphs: Reading in a language you are learning is one of the best ways to become fluent. Instead of stopping at every word you do not know, switching to an external dictionary, and being unsure if the meaning stays the same in context, Leggio unobtrusively delivers the right meaning as an elegant tooltip within the text, so the reading can go on.

uses.title: Learners
items: Reading the news in the language you’re learning, like Le Monde, El País, or NHK Easy, without switching tabs.
Working through a novel or short story as a PDF, for example Pinocchio in Italian or Borges in Spanish, and building a word list as you go.
Reading Reddit, forums, or recipe blogs in the language you’re learning, so practice fits into ordinary browsing.
Exporting saved words to CSV and importing them into Anki or Quizlet for spaced repetition.
Heritage speakers who understand a language but can’t read it well, catching up on the written form.

uses.title: Students and academics
items: Graduate students reading sources in a language they read slowly, such as German philosophy, French theory, or Spanish archival documents.
Getting through reading-knowledge language exams for PhD programs.
Historians working with scanned foreign-language documents, using OCR on the page.

uses.title: Work and travel

name: GREATERCIRCLE
blurb: An interactive globe built for anyone curious about how we really fly. While standard flight maps draw straight lines from point A to point B, this tool calculates the true great-circle distance between any two points, factoring in political geography and user preference. Simply place your points, note the regions or airspace to avoid, and watch the program plot out the optimal route.
tagline: An interactive globe that plots the shortest flight route between two places, around the regions you want to avoid.

sections.title: Technical details
paragraphs: The route improves on great circle distance pathfinding on a sphere by calculating a chain of great-circle arcs bending only at the avoided regions' convex corners, found by an A* algorithm over their tangent visibility graph, in three-dimensional unit vectors.
Borders from Natural Earth; places from GeoNames and OurAirports, with Photon for the long tail. Labeled cities come from a modified GaWC index.

sections.title: Inspiration
paragraphs: I was flying from South Korea to Poland and not long after takeoff, I booted up the seat-back flight map to see that our plane was projected to chart a straight line through four countries with closed off airspaces. As a nervous flier, knowing the accurate flight path would have put me more at ease.
